description:
I’m passionate about scientific research, mathematics, and technology, with experience in developing research projects and solving complex problems.

I’m building a team for NASA’s Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge and looking for motivated members with skills in programming, physics, engineering, data analysis, space science, or UI/UX design.

If you’re curious, committed, and ready to contribute your ideas and skills, join our team and let’s build something meaningful together!
summary:
LUNAR ΔV is the team that created a web-based tool that helps mission planners compare Moon south pole landing sites and dates. Near the pole, the Sun and Earth sit only a few degrees above the horizon, so a single ridge can decide whether a lander has solar power or a direct-to-Earth communication link.

We built an interactive app that combines NASA/JPL ephemerides with NASA LOLA terrain. For each site, it computes the share of time in sunlight and with Earth in view, the longest darkness, and the longest communication gap. Results appear as a ranking, a sky diagram over the terrain skyline, a timeline, and a 3D terrain view lit by the Sun.

A Mission Planner lets users enter what their mission needs, such as minimum sunlight, communication time and maximum darkness. The tool shows which sites qualify, finds the best landing window, and checks solar power and battery sizing. An exportable assurance record documents the assumptions, data sources and a result hash for mission reviews.

LUNAR ΔV matters because choosing where and when to land is costly, risky and hard to explain. Our tool makes that decision faster to explore and easier to understand for planners, educators, students and the public.
details:
Project Details

What it does and how it works

CLPS-NASA-Space-Apps-Final is a web tool for comparing Moon south pole landing sites. Near the pole, the Sun and Earth skim only a few degrees above the horizon, so a single ridge can decide whether a lander has power or can talk to Earth. CLPS-NASA-Space-Apps-Final shows this at a glance.

A planner picks 2 to 4 sites (from a list, a south pole map, or custom coordinates) and a date range of up to one year. The app computes the Sun’s and Earth’s azimuth and elevation from NASA/JPL ephemerides and compares them against each site’s terrain horizon, built from NASA LOLA elevation data. It reports:

  • the share of time in sunlight and with Earth in view
  • the longest darkness
  • the longest communication gap
  • a ranking of the sites

Results appear as a sky diagram over the terrain silhouette, a timeline, and a 3D terrain view lit by the Sun at the selected time. A Mission Planner section lets users enter what their mission needs. Profiles include CLPS 14 days, Artemis-class 7 days, and Rover 28 days, or users can set their own. The tool then shows which sites meet those needs and finds the best landing window. It also checks solar power and battery sizing, and exports an assurance record (a JSON file with assumptions, sources and a SHA-256 hash) for mission reviews.

Benefits

  • Replaces days of specialist analysis with seconds of interactive comparison.
  • Plain-language Simple mode for students and the public, and Expert mode for engineers.
  • Open, transparent assumptions. Every result states which horizon model was used.
  • Available in English and Arabic.

Intended impact

We want to make lunar landing site selection understandable and accessible. Mission planners can screen sites and dates faster. Educators and the public can see why the south pole is hard. Teams can document their reasoning with an exportable record.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js (3D Moon and terrain)
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Matplotlib, Pillow
  • Data and science: NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels, JPL Horizons, NASA LOLA digital elevation models, NASA SVS Moon imagery
  • Infrastructure: Docker Compose, nginx. It runs on a normal laptop, with no special hardware.

Creative side

  • A Mission Planner that starts from mission requirements and tells you where and when to land, instead of only showing plots.
  • Terrain-aware sunlight: a site counts as lit when any part of the Sun’s disc clears the skyline, and the horizon switch shows how often terrain flips the ranking.
  • A daily feasibility calendar and a first-order power and battery check.
  • Shareable links that encode the whole scenario.
  • A combined design: two analysis engines (CLPS and Shackleton Navigator) with a badge showing which one produced each result.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: visibility is geometric (line of sight), not RF link quality, and this is a research and education prototype, not flight certification. This is stated in the app.
  • Terrain: real LOLA terrain matters, so it is on by default and can be switched off to compare.
  • Accessibility: two modes, a bilingual interface, and a mobile layout.
  • Reproducibility: an assurance export with assumptions, data sources and a result hash.
  • Limits: the sample sites are placeholders until the official candidate list is loaded, and some tools need LOLA DEM paths configured.
